page_text.main_text_caveat: These correlations describe how the share of electricity customers without power and the share of cell sites out move together across county-reports within a storm. Both may follow the storm's path and strength, so the correlation does not show how much one drives the other.
page_text.lag_pattern: Cell outages line up about as closely with power outages 6 hours earlier (median correlation 0.60) as with power outages at the same time (0.61), and less closely with power outages 24 hours earlier (0.36).
page_text.methods_denominator_note: EAGLE-I's modeled customer count is below EAGLE-I's own recorded outages in 249 of 2,331 storm-counties (for example, Henderson County, North Carolina: 24 modeled customers, 131,460 customers out, 49,494 households). Those storm-counties are left out of every % of customers result; using households as the denominator instead is shown as a sensitivity.
page_text.no_exposure_model: Chapter 6 fits no model that controls for exposure; the plan does not include one.

notes: EAGLE-I 'customers' are electricity meters, not people or households.
EAGLE-I covers 2014-2025, so storms in 2026 (Isaias) have no power match or overlay until a 2026 release exists.
Co-movement is a Spearman rank correlation across county-reports within a storm; it describes how the two move together, not why.
Counties whose EAGLE-I modeled customer count is below EAGLE-I's own recorded outages are left out of % of customers.
Every result carries its count by EAGLE-I coverage flag; low_coverage = the state's minimum covered share below 0.75 that year.

page_text.storm_misses: Here a storm's peak share pools each county's own peak report, so it can differ from the single-report peak in chapter 3. Held out of the fit, with misses of 5 percentage points or more listed, storms' pooled peak shares were higher than predicted for Ida (28.8% observed, 9.4% predicted), Helene (13.5% observed, 8.3% predicted) and Irma (27.0% observed, 17.9% predicted); and lower than predicted for Idalia (2.3% observed, 8.2% predicted), Nicholas (2.4% observed, 15.1% predicted), Nate (0.1% observed, 8.8% predicted) and Nicole (1.2% observed, 10.0% predicted). Flooding, road access and fiber cuts are possible unmeasured factors; this design cannot tell whether they, or something else, account for the gaps.

original.headline: In this data, counties with higher social vulnerability did not take measurably longer for cell outages to fall below 5% of sites. The estimates rule out a large delay for the most vulnerable quartile (a rate of recovery more than 4% slower), though they can't rule out a smaller one.
original.headline_bound: For the most vulnerable quartile, the 95% interval for the hazard ratio runs from 0.97 to 1.55: a rate of falling below 5% more than 4% lower than the least vulnerable quartile's is outside it; a smaller shortfall, or a rate up to 55% higher, is not.

landfall_or_closest_approach.headline: In this data, counties with higher social vulnerability did not take measurably longer for cell outages to fall below 5% of sites. The estimates rule out a large delay for the most vulnerable quartile (a rate of recovery more than 3% slower), though they can't rule out a smaller one.
landfall_or_closest_approach.headline_bound: For the most vulnerable quartile, the 95% interval for the hazard ratio runs from 0.97 to 1.57: a rate of falling below 5% more than 3% lower than the least vulnerable quartile's is outside it; a smaller shortfall, or a rate up to 56% higher, is not.
landfall_or_closest_approach.note: day 0: the earlier of the first study-state landfall and the closest approach to the study-state counties (first 2026-11-23 rule)

page_text.headline: In this data, counties with higher social vulnerability did not take measurably longer for cell outages to fall below 5% of sites. The estimates rule out a large delay for the most vulnerable quartile (a rate of recovery more than 5% slower), though they can't rule out a smaller one.
page_text.headline_bound: For the most vulnerable quartile, the 95% interval for the hazard ratio runs from 0.95 to 1.53: a rate of falling below 5% more than 5% lower than the least vulnerable quartile's is outside it; a smaller shortfall, or a rate up to 53% higher, is not.
page_text.best_case_sensitivity: Sensitivity display, not a finding: if counties that leave the reports while still out are counted as having fallen below 5% at their next unreported report, the third and fourth quartiles reach it sooner (hazard ratios 1.36 [1.08, 1.72] and 1.35 [1.08, 1.68]). The difference disappears if those counties are instead kept at risk to the storm's last report (1.09 [0.88, 1.36] and 1.12 [0.89, 1.41]).
page_text.wording: Associations only: these results describe how long counties in each SVI quartile took to fall below 5% of sites out. They do not show why, and say nothing about anyone's intent.
cannot_rule_out: SVI is correlated with rurality, terrain and network density; any of these, or other differences between counties, may be associated with both SVI and restoration times.
Public DIRS tables combine all providers, so differences between providers' networks in different counties cannot be seen.
Counties that leave the reports while still out are censored; if leaving the reports differs by SVI quartile, the comparison can shift (see the best and worst cases).
Wind zone, distance and track-point wind do not capture flooding, road access or fiber cuts.

notes: Quartiles are of the at-risk storm-counties' SVI 2022 national percentiles; national cut points are a sensitivity display.
Hazard ratios above 1 mean a county reaches below 5% of sites out sooner than the lowest-SVI quartile, holding exposure and storm fixed.
The event is the first report from which a county stays below 5% in every later report that includes it.

wording.note: At least one of the plan's red flags is triggered, so this chapter makes no statement about whether recovery changed after the rules. It shows each storm and each period's median and range, and lists the flags.

page_text.headline: The public reports can't yet show whether the FCC's 2024–2025 rules coincided with any change in recovery: one rule period has no storm, another has only Isaias, and the sites-served counts shift within storms by as much as 31%.

notes: Descriptive only: no regression, test, p-value, hazard ratio or adjusted difference between periods.
With few storms per period, this is association, not proof.
Times to 90% are given under both treatments of counties that leave the reports.
Rule periods: MDRI from May 1, 2024; mandatory DIRS from February 20, 2025 (DA 25-74); FCC 26-34's changes from June 30, 2026 (Federal Register publication). Checked 2026-11-22.
